title: The Scaling and Profitability Trade off: Venture Capital's Weakest Link!
gist: Aswath Damodaran argues venture capital's scale-first-profits-later default is an incentive artifact, not a business truth: VCs price rather than value, and with 80% of 2023-26 VC returns coming from the top 1% of investments, the power law pushes them to chase scale and exit before business-model flaws surface. Public money flooding private markets (the 'gray market') plus a decayed mean-reversion effect in public equities has stretched the median IPO to older, bigger, and mostly unprofitable, with Facebook's $104bn 2012 pricing giving way to SpaceX at $1.8 trillion in June 2026 and Anthropic/OpenAI pitching trillion-dollar-plus valuations on ARR growth alone.

insights.claim: Scalability is set by market-side variables a company mostly does not control — market size, market growth, industry structure, capital intensity, customer inertia and key-person dependence — so scaling ambition is a business-model question, not a management-willpower question.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Score any growth story against these six variables before underwriting a scaling narrative; a company scaling against unfavorable structure is burning capital, not compounding it.
insights.locator: The Scaling Choice

insights.claim: Profitability is driven by a separate set of forces from scalability — unit economics, economies of scale where fixed costs do not grow with revenue, and moats that confer pricing power — which is why revenue growth does not mechanically convert into earnings.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Model scale and margin as two independent axes; a name can win the scale axis and still be structurally uninvestable on the margin axis.
insights.quote: scaling up is not a mantra that automatically translates in profitability
insights.locator: Business Building

insights.claim: Software-type businesses convert scale into profit because the marginal unit costs almost nothing to produce yet can be priced highly, while businesses like electric cars, where each incremental unit carries real cost, struggle to convert scaled revenue into profit.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Unit economics, not TAM, decides whether a growth cohort's losses are investment or leakage — apply this split when comparing AI software to hardware-heavy scalers.
insights.locator: Unit economics : Unit economics measures the profitability

insights.claim: How a company defines its own market materially changes its scaling ceiling — describing Uber as a logistics company covering car service, moving and delivery rather than just a car service company could triple its potential market.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Watch for TAM redefinition in pitch decks: it is a legitimate value lever but also the cheapest way to inflate a scaling story without changing the business.
insights.locator: Market size : It is easier to scale up a company

insights.claim: The smartphone market's tailwind for scaling has fully dissipated — a handset maker in 2010 could grow by converting flip-phone users and penetrating emerging markets, but by 2026 the market has matured and growth must be taken from competitors' customers.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Scaling stories in mature end-markets require share-take assumptions, which are far less reliable than market-growth assumptions — discount them accordingly.
insights.locator: Market growth : It is also easier to scale up

insights.claim: Uber's early scaling was cheap specifically because it owned no cars and hired no drivers, making growth possible with little added investment — capital intensity is the hinge between fast and slow scaling.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Asset-light structure buys scaling speed but does not buy unit economics; separate the two when a platform's growth decelerates.
insights.locator: Capital intensity : It is easier to scale up a business

insights.claim: Operating choices trade the two axes against each other directly: cutting prices raises revenue while damaging unit economics, and raising advertising spend expands the market while dragging on profitability.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Read growth acceleration alongside gross margin and S&M intensity — accelerating revenue with deteriorating both is bought growth, not earned growth.
insights.locator: It is true that the operating choices that businesses make

insights.claim: Businesses that scale up fastest also tend to scale down fastest, making rapid scaling itself a marker of fragility rather than durability.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Treat velocity of revenue ramp as a risk input, not just a quality signal, when sizing positions in hypergrowth names.
insights.quote: the businesses that scale up quickly often scale down just as fast
insights.locator: As you can see, some businesses can scale up quickly

insights.claim: Simultaneous fast scaling and real profitability — the 'Lightning in a Bottle' outcome exemplified by early Google and Facebook — requires a rare four-way coincidence: a big growing market, early entry with few competitors, low capital intensity and excellent unit economics.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Use this four-condition checklist to test whether a company claiming the Google/Facebook path actually has the preconditions, or is just borrowing the analogy.
insights.locator: Lightning in a Bottle: Are scaling and profitability mutually exclusive?

insights.claim: Amazon's 'Field of Dreams' model worked because it disrupted a huge retail business that had atrophied and weakened over time, not because scale-first is generalizable — the imitators that copied the growth dimension had neither the unit economics nor the economies of scale to turn the corner on profitability.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The 'next Amazon' comparison is only valid if the target industry is both huge and structurally weakened; otherwise the cohort is a Field of Nightmares.
insights.locator: Field of Nightmares: Amazon was not the first successful

insights.claim: Deliberately staying small can be the value-maximizing choice — Ferrari sells only a few thousand cars a year but with an operating margin above 20% trades at a market capitalization comparable to automakers selling hundreds of thousands of cars.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Niche dominance with premium pricing can support revenue and earnings multiples that scale-chasers never reach — a template for screening small, high-margin, moated names.
insights.locator: Niche Star : Scaling is not always the optimal choice

insights.claim: WeWork's model of leasing property long term and sub-leasing it short term carried a fatal duration mismatch, and scaling it geographically across hundreds of properties converted a bad small business into a bad large one rather than fixing it.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Structural mismatches do not amortize with scale — screen for models where growth multiplies the flaw instead of diluting it.
insights.quote: has a duration mismatch born in hell, and expanding it geographically and allowing it to lease hundreds of properties, as WeWork did, just makes it a really big, bad business
insights.locator: Big and Broken : It is no secret that there are some businesses

insights.claim: Continued capital infusions into businesses that can neither scale nor make money do not prevent failure — they only delay it and raise its final price tag.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Bridge rounds into structurally broken models are value-destroying for late money; watch for down-round dynamics where the loss is being deferred, not avoided.
insights.locator: Cut your losses: Finally, there are businesses that start up with dreams aplenty

insights.claim: Applying scale-first-profit-later as a universal rulebook rather than a situational choice systematically converts small business failures into large ones.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The cost of the cookbook approach shows up as larger absolute write-downs across a VC cohort, not more winners.
insights.quote: runs the risk of making small failures into big ones
insights.locator: Any investor or founder who blindly follows the pathway of scaling first

themes.theme: Founder psychology as a valuation variable

insights.claim: The choice to scale or stay small is frequently driven by founder personality rather than economics — some founders refuse economically sensible growth because equity or debt financing dilutes their control, while others scale aggressively out of ambition even when fundamentals do not support expansion.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Founder control preferences are a real input to terminal-value assumptions; the Founder's Dilemma predicts when a scaling plan requires the founder to step back.
insights.locator: Control versus Ambition : There is a natural tension

insights.claim: Longevity and scale are in tension — some of the world's longest-lived firms are small family-owned niche businesses passed down through generations, while firms that scale up overnight on a windfall often do lasting damage to their business models.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Sudden revenue surges are a warning about future capital allocation, not just a positive earnings revision.
insights.locator: Longevity versus Scale : There is an argument to be made

insights.claim: Moderna and Peloton both boomed in the aftermath of the Covid shutdown and then overreached, doing long-term damage to their business models by scaling to a demand level that was external and temporary.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Named precedent for the pattern of windfall-driven overexpansion — apply the same test to any current cohort scaling on a demand shock.
insights.locator: In the aftermath of the Covid shutdown

insights.claim: Vinod Khosla's public claim that every business should put scaling ahead of profitability likely confuses profitability with cash flows, yet that prioritization is the norm rather than the exception among venture capitalists and has become more pronounced over the last two decades.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The scale-first doctrine is an industry consensus worth fading at the portfolio level, not a settled finding about business building.
insights.locator: Vinod Khosla is one of those legends

insights.claim: Any business that seeks outside capital — family, venture or public equity — must accept that providers get a say in decisions, and the more capital raised, the more sway they hold.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Capital-raising cadence is a leading indicator of which party's incentives will drive strategy — track cumulative dilution as a governance signal.
insights.locator: The bottom line is that businesses that seek out capital

themes.theme: VC incentives and the power law

insights.claim: Venture capitalists price companies rather than value them, benchmarking against what other VCs pay for similar businesses using simplistic metrics — users and subscribers for pre-revenue firms, forward revenues or earnings otherwise.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Private marks are relative-pricing artifacts, not intrinsic values, so a repricing of the peer set cascades through an entire portfolio at once.
insights.locator: There are two parts of the venture capital rulebook

insights.claim: VC success is measured on entry price versus exit price rather than the quality of the business built, which is the structural reason VCs have little incentive to fix broken business models before exiting.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Do not expect VC board presence to function as business-quality discipline; the metric they are judged on rewards a clean exit, not a durable company.
insights.quote: VC success is measured based on price at entry and price at exit on an investment, rather than the quality of the business built
insights.locator: The second is that VC success is measured based on price at entry

insights.claim: On Cambridge Associates data, the median venture capitalist has not harvested materially more alpha than the median mutual fund manager or private equity investor, undercutting the premium narrative around the asset class.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Allocators paying VC-level fees for median exposure are buying illiquidity without the excess return — manager selection is the entire proposition.
insights.locator: the median venture capitalist has not been much better at harvesting alpha

insights.claim: Returns concentration in venture capital has intensified to an extreme: in the 2023-2026 period, 80% of all returns to VC investors came from the top 1% of investments, up from a historical pattern where the top 10% carried the bulk of returns.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: At 1%-tail dependence, a diversified VC fund without a top-decile deal is mathematically an underperformer — this is the number to cite when sizing venture allocations.
insights.quote: in the 2023-2026 period, 80% of all returns to VC investors came from their top 1% of investments
insights.locator: As you can see, across all the time periods

insights.claim: Failure is more intrinsic to venture capital than to other asset classes — more VC funds go out of existence each year, and even the most successful funds lose money on many or most of their investments, especially angel-stage deals.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Loss rates are the base case, so due diligence on the winner-selection process matters far more than average portfolio quality.
insights.quote: not only are there more VC funds that go out of existence every year, but even the most successful VC funds lose on many or even most of the investments that they make
insights.locator: The first is that failure, always a concern in investing

insights.claim: Only about a quarter of venture capitalists in any given year deliver above-average returns, yet unlike in mutual funds and hedge funds where outperformance is fleeting, VC success has been more enduring across cycles.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Persistence justifies paying up for access to established top-quartile VC franchises while treating the rest of the field as beta with worse liquidity.
insights.locator: The first is that only about a quarter of venture capitalists

insights.claim: The more top-heavy VC returns become, the more pressure venture capitalists feel and pass on to portfolio companies to find the next big winner, pushing the ecosystem dangerously close to gambling.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Rising return concentration is self-reinforcing: it mechanically increases risk-taking at portfolio companies, so concentration data is a leading indicator of ecosystem fragility.
insights.quote: pushing the ecosystem dangerously close to gambling
insights.locator: The power law characteristic also feeds into VC incentives

insights.claim: Given how venture capitalists invest, act and are judged, it is unrealistic to expect them to do the heavy lifting of long-term business building — the gap between what VCs are assumed to do and what they actually do is structural rather than a matter of character.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Strip the 'sherpa' premium out of any thesis that relies on VC stewardship to fix a portfolio company's economics.
insights.locator: If you are reading this as a critique of venture capitalists

themes.theme: The gray market: public money in private deals

insights.claim: Public-market capital has crossed into private financing — mutual funds like T. Rowe Price and Fidelity invested billions in high-profile private tech companies including Uber, joined by sovereign funds investing directly or through vehicles like Softbank's Vision fund.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Mutual fund holders now carry pre-IPO mark-to-model risk inside supposedly liquid funds — check private allocations in growth-fund holdings.
insights.locator: The Gray Market Effect

insights.claim: The merger of VC and public-equity capital pools into a single 'gray market' is what allows private businesses to stay private for far longer, dissolving the old separation between a private market for young firms and a public market for mature ones.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Value creation now happens before listing, so public-market investors buying IPOs are buying a later, more expensive slice of the life cycle.
insights.locator: In effect, rather than two mostly separated markets

insights.claim: Some growth businesses now bypass venture capital altogether for public equity or strategic investment from large mature companies, whose motives vary from technology access to pre-empting competitors to pure financial return.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Strategic corporate capital carries different exit incentives than VC — identify which type funded a private name before assuming a standard IPO path.
insights.locator: Public equity: There are some growth businesses that bypass venture capital

themes.theme: Weakening mean reversion in public markets

insights.claim: In markets that function properly, scaling feeds momentum while profitability acts as the fundamental anchor that produces reversals, but evidence from Ken French's datasets shows the reversal effect has weakened over time, leaving mean-reversion bettors stranded.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The historical counterweight to momentum is decaying, so value strategies relying on price reversal need a catalyst rather than patience.
insights.quote: there is evidence that the reversal effect has weakened over time, leaving investors who bet on mean reversion and a return to fundamentals in the lurch
insights.locator: Public Markets: Momentum, Fundamentals and Reversals

insights.claim: Passive investing now holds well above 50% of the market, and its flows disproportionately reach the largest market-cap companies while shrinking the population of active investors who scrutinize business models and profitability.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: A mechanical bid for the largest caps plus fewer fundamental scrutineers is a structural argument for momentum persistence in mega-caps.
insights.locator: The rise of passive investing : In the battle between active investing and passive investing

insights.claim: The reversal effect began weakening in the 1990s, the decade when dot-com companies with unformed business models flooded public markets, because firms whose value rests entirely on potential rather than current operating metrics lack the near-term catalysts that trigger reversal.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Market composition, not just monetary policy, explains momentum dominance — expect reversion to stay weak while pre-profit listings dominate the growth cohort.
insights.locator: Public market composition : It is noteworthy that the reversal effect started weakening

insights.claim: Damodaran takes issue with parts of each standard explanation for weakening reversals — the Fed's low rates, passive flows, market composition and faster uncurated information — but accepts all four carry some truth, making pushing back against momentum a more hazardous exercise.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: No single fix restores reversion, so treat contrarian positioning against momentum as a higher-risk trade than the historical record implies.
insights.locator: While I take issue with parts of each of these arguments

insights.claim: Companies going public in the United States are waiting materially longer, with the median age at IPO rising about 11 years over the last 15 years according to Jay Ritter's IPO data.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Longer private tenure means public investors get later-stage entry points — a structural drag on IPO-cohort forward returns.
insights.locator: 1. Private businesses are waiting longer before going public

insights.claim: Inflation-adjusted revenues at the median US IPO have tripled or quadrupled relative to IPOs in the 1980s, so companies now list far bigger than they used to.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Scale at listing has increased even as quality has fallen — revenue size is no longer a proxy for IPO maturity.
insights.locator: 2. Private businesses are scaling up (revenues) more, while waiting

insights.claim: Profitability at IPO has collapsed: over 80% of companies going public in the 1980s were profitable, versus less than a quarter of companies that have gone public in the last decade.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The single hardest number in the piece: today's IPO buyer is underwriting a business model that mostly does not yet exist.
insights.quote: less that a quarter of the companies that have gone public in the last decade have been profitable
insights.locator: 3. Private businesses are deferring building business models & profitability

insights.claim: Companies going public are issuing smaller portions of their shares in the initial offering, suggesting the capital need that historically drove listings has become less pressing because private capital access improved.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Smaller floats mean thinner price discovery and larger lockup-expiry supply shocks — a tradeable feature of the modern IPO calendar.
insights.locator: You will also notice that companies going public are issuing smaller portions

insights.claim: The median market cap of a US company going public in the last six years has exceeded a billion dollars, and the largest IPOs run from Facebook's $104 billion pricing in 2012 to SpaceX going public in June 2026 at $1.8 trillion.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Listing valuations have escalated by more than an order of magnitude in 14 years, compressing the post-IPO return runway public investors used to capture.
insights.quote: From Facebook, with a pricing of $104 billion, in 2012 to SpaceX, going public in June 2026 at $1.8 trillion, the trend lines are pointing upwards
insights.locator: While the median market cap of a company going public in the last six years

insights.claim: The escalation in listing valuations is set to continue if Anthropic and OpenAI deliver on their trillion-dollar-plus pricing promise.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The next two mega-listings are the test of whether public markets will absorb trillion-dollar pre-profit pricing.
insights.locator: especially if Anthropic and OpenAI deliver on their trillion-dollar

insights.claim: Deferred listings mean governance scrutiny is deferred too, producing companies priced at a billion, hundreds of billions or even trillions run by people facing few checks, since founder worship and divide-and-conquer dynamics neutralize VCs as a disciplinary mechanism.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Governance risk is now concentrated in the largest private names — a key-person or conduct event there has no public-market circuit breaker.
insights.quote: you can have companies with market pricing of a billion, hundreds of billions or even trillions run by people who are ill-suited for the task
insights.locator: Corporate governance: One of the reasons that private companies often delay going public

insights.claim: Scaling first and building the business model later can be irreversible, because the operating choices made to enable rapid scaling may themselves block the eventual pathway to profitability.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Path dependency means a company's cost structure may be permanently mis-set — do not assume margins can be 'switched on' once growth slows.
insights.locator: Delayed business model building: If the first imperative for a private business

insights.claim: The Anthropic sales pitch consists mainly of annualized revenue run-rate growth and an unspecified but huge AI market size, with little or no mention of business models or profitability — an incomplete story focused almost entirely on scaling.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: ARR-plus-TAM is the tell of a pure scaling narrative; demand unit economics before underwriting AI-company valuations at these levels.
insights.quote: in the Anthropic sales pitch it is the growth in the annualized revenue run rate (ARR) and the size of the AI market (huge, but with no specifics) that comprises the bulk of the story
insights.locator: Scaling stories : If you believe, as I do, that valuation is a bridge

insights.claim: Supplying near-endless capital to disruptors without challenging their business models can produce disruption without replacement, where incumbents are driven out but the disruptor never builds a self-sustaining business.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: A destroyed incumbent industry plus an unprofitable disruptor is a net negative for the sector — watch for capacity that never gets rebuilt.
insights.quote: your disruptor may not be able to build a business that can be self-sustaining in the long term
insights.locator: Disruption without replacement : Disruption has been a key component

insights.claim: It is possible that companies both public and private carrying sky-high pricing today have been built on bad business models that are irredeemable, because changes in private and public capital markets have tilted incentives further toward scaling.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: The author's closing risk call: treat scale-driven valuations in today's largest pre-profit names as potentially unrecoverable, not merely early.
insights.quote: it is possible that companies, both public and private, with sky-high pricing have been built on bad business models that are irredeemable
insights.locator: Conclusion

insights.claim: Valuation is a bridge between stories and numbers whose balance shifts over the life cycle — stories dominate early and numbers take center stage later — which is why founders and VCs marketing young companies are primarily storytellers.
insights.speaker: Aswath Damodaran
insights.so_what: Judge a young company's pitch on story completeness (does it address margins and moats?), and demand numeric proof as the company ages.
insights.locator: Scaling stories : If you believe, as I do, that valuation is a bridge
